title: 19  Backpropagation
text:
19.1 Simple example
In this section, we will explore backpropagation in more depth. This method is used to compute the gradient of a neural network’s loss function with respect to its parameters, which allows us to use gradient descent (?sec-optimisation) to minimise the loss function.
As an example, we can consider a network comprising a single node, with the loss defined as mean squared error. We can write the loss in terms of the weights, as follows :
\[
\begin{align}
L&=(\hat{y}-y)^2 \\\\
\hat{y}&=f(z) \\\\
z&=\alpha x + \beta
\end{align}
\]
It should be clear that the derivative of the loss with respect to the weight, \(\alpha\), can now be computed using the chain rule :
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha} =
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}}
\frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial z}
\frac{\partial z}{\partial \alpha}
\]
By computing each derivativ in turn : \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}} &= 2(\hat{y}-y) \\\\
\frac{\partial z}{\partial \alpha} &= x
\end{align}
\]
We find that :
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha} =
2(\hat{y}-y) f'(z) x
\]
And similarly :
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \beta} =
2(\hat{y}-y) f'(z)
\]
Note that in backpropagation, we are not trying to find a closed-form solution for the derivative, but just to establish an efficient method for computing the numerical values. We find that, provided the derivative of the activation function, \(f'(z)\), is known, the derivative of the loss can be computed using only the values of \(x\), \(y\), \(\hat{y}\) and \(z\). These terms are all calculated during the forward pass, making this an efficient method for computing the gradient of the loss.

title: 19  Backpropagation
text:
19.2 Extension to multiple layers
Now consider a network comprising multiple layers. We will denote the output (aka activation) of the \(i\)-th layer as \(a_i\), with corresponding subscripts on weights and biases. So the final layer of an \(n\) layer network can be written :
\[
a_n = f(\alpha_n a_{n-1} + \beta_n)
\]
The derivative of the loss for this final layer, remains as above :
\[
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha_n} &=
2(a_n-y) f'(z_n) a_{n-1} \\\\
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \beta_n} &=
2(a_n-y) f'(z_n)
\end{align}
\]
For the previous layer, we must expand \(a_{n-1}\) using the activation function of that layer, ie.
\[
a_{n-1} = f(\alpha_{n-1}a_{n-2} + \beta_{n-1})
\]
Which means the derivative of the loss with respect to weights in this \((n-1)\)-th layer becomes :
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha_{n-1}} =
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a_n}
\frac{\partial a_n}{\partial z_n}
\frac{\partial z_n}{\partial a_{n-1}}
\frac{\partial a_{n-1}}{\partial \alpha_{n-1}}
\]
which can again be written in terms that are computed during the forward pass :
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha_n} =
2(a_n-y) f'(z_n) \alpha_n x_{n-2}
\]
It should now be clear that we can compute all partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each weight, by starting with the final layer and working backwards. Hence the term backpropagation.

title: 19  Backpropagation
text:
19.3 Extension to multivariate functions
In practice, our networks have multiple input and output variables, represented as vectors, and the weights become matrices. The chain rule still applies, but the derivatives become Jacobian matrices, and the “multiplication” becomes matrix multiplication. The multivariate chain rule states that the Jacobian of a function composition is the matrix product of the individual Jacobians:
\[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{z}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{z}}{\partial \mathbf{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}
\]
where \(\mathbf{y} = f(\mathbf{x})\) and \(\mathbf{z} = g(\mathbf{y})\).

19.3.1 Automatic Differentiation
Modern deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX — see Section 18.5) don’t compute derivatives symbolically or numerically; instead they use automatic differentiation. Given a function implemented in a computer program, automatic differentiation computes the derivative of that function with respect to its inputs, by applying the chain rule to the sequence of elementary operations that make up the function. When the function is called, theframework records the sequence of operations performed, and stores the intermediate values which are then used to compute the derivative using backpropagation.

title: 20  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
20.1 Introduction to CNNs
So far in this course the neural networks we have mostly been working with have been types of Multilayer Perceptron (MLPs). These foundational neural networks are not suited to all types of problem. One such example involves images, i.e. a set of pixels - these will be treated independently, ignoring the spatial structure of the data. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were developed to address this issue Lecun, Bottou, Bengio, & Haffner (1998).

title: 20  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
20.2 How do CNNs work
The building blocks of a CNN are:

Convolutional Layer
Activation Layer
Pooling Layer
Fully connected layer


20.2.1 Convolutional Layer
This layer performs the core mathematical function - a sliding window is shiftd across the image looking for specific features. These sliding windows are called filters or kernels and there are several which are each looking for different patterns e.g. straight lines or curves. The filters highlight the specific pattern they are looking for and create a feature map. Activation functions are used to ensure non-linear transformations are possible in the network, e.g. by ReLu is commonly used in the convolutional layers in a CNN.






Figure 20.1: The convolutional layer outputs a feature map





20.2.2 Pooling Layer
This layer’s primary purpose is to identify the most significant features and reduce the size of the feature maps. A filter is used which scans over the feature map and aggregation functions are used to reduce the dimensionality of the data. Types of aggregation function include:

Max Pooling: Selects the maximum value from the area of the feature map covered by the filter
Average Pooling: Calculates the average value within the area of the feature map and uses this to select significant features







Figure 20.2: The pooling layer identifies significant features





20.2.3 Fully connected Layer
This layer is there to assign final predictions based on the outputs of the previous convolution and pooling layers. Each node in this layer is connected to each node in the previous layer. In a classification task the activation function is typically SoftMax, which turns the flatted vector of features into a probability distribution.






Figure 20.3: The fully connected layer assigns final predictions

title: 20  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
20.3 CNN parameters

20.3.1 Stride
The stride is the number of pixels that the convolutional filter moves each time it starts a new pass. A stride of 1 means one pixel at a time, 2 means two pixels at a time etc. This parameter has an important effect on the performance of a CNN. Larger strides reduce spatial dimensions of the output feature map, while increasing computational efficiency. However they can also miss fine-grained features while capturing the broad ones.


20.3.2 Padding
In fixed size images there will be edges of the image where the convolutional filter can not be applied; this can lead to a loss of information. Padding adds extra pixels around the image, usually just zeros, which allow the filter to be applied - without adding artifical information.

title: 20  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
20.4 Limitations of CNNs
CNNs, although very powerful for datasets composed of images, do have their limitations. The networks are frequently complex which take significant resources to train, along with having to use large datasets to be performant. Another issue that commonly occurs is known as the vanising gradient problem which occurs with deeper networks. As the gradients become smaller between layers it becomes more difficult for earlier layers to learn. In fact it was shown that deeper networks, which were orignally thought to be more performant, were actually exhibiting signs of poorer performance than shallower ones, with higher training and test errors.

title: 20  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
20.5 Deep Residual Learning
He, Zhang, Ren, & Sun (2015) proposed a new structure for CNNs which helped to alleviate some of the issues described above. They key shift was to use skipped connections to speed up training, which also had the benefit of preventing the vanishing gradient problem.

20.5.1 ResNet basic idea
The idea behind this network architecture can be described simply mathematically. Instead of learning:
\[
\begin{align}
y=f(x)
\end{align}
\]
the network learns
\[
\begin{align}
y=f(x) + x.
\end{align}
\]
The network learns the correction needed for the mapping rather than the full mapping itself. If we consider a simple mapping of:
\[
\begin{align}
y=x
\end{align}
\]
a standard network will try to learn:
\[
\begin{align}
f(x)=x
\end{align}
\]
rather than
\[
\begin{align}
f(x)=0
\end{align}
\] .
It is easier for the network to learn f(x)=0 than learn how to map the identity function directly.


20.5.2 Skipped connections
The identity function is a key concept in residual networks. By using shortcut connections or skipped connections - which perform identity mapping - the outputs can be added to the outputs of intermediate layers. The original x is copied forward unchanged and new features are added to this - corrections.






Figure 20.4: The pooling layer identifies significant features



To summarise, with a standard CNN each layer is relearning lots of information again and has to re-encode this information. Using a ResNet architecture keeps previous information and only learns what has changed.




He, K., Zhang, X., Ren, S., & Sun, J. (2015). Deep residual learning for image recognition. Retrieved from https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385


Lecun, Y., Bottou, L., Bengio, Y., & Haffner, P. (1998). Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition. https://doi.org/10.1109/5.726791

title: 21  Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
21.1 Recurrent Unit
So far we have studied networks for which the input comprises an N-dimensional vector per data point. A broad category of data which does not easily conform to this representation is sequential or time-series data. Examples include text, speech, weather, financial markets. Recurrent neural networks are a broad category of neural network that are designed to handle this type of data.
The defining feature of recurrent networks is that they store some hidden state between data points. The most simple example is the “recurrent unit”, illustrated schematically in Figure 21.1. The hidden state, \(h\), is computed for each input data point \(x\), and depends on the previous value of \(h\). We can write this algebraically as :
\[
\begin{align}
h_t &= f_1(\alpha x_t + \beta h_{t-1} + \gamma) \\
y_t &= f_2(\theta h_t + \lambda)
\end{align}
\]
where \(h_t\) is the hidden state for time step \(t\), \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are activation functions, and \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \theta, \lambda\) are weights and biases.
Another useful way to illustrate the recurrent unit is shown in Figure 21.2. Note that this does not show a network, instead it illustrates the calculations performed by a single recurrent unit over several time steps.
Here the input data sequence \(x_0, x_1, ... x_t, ... , x_n\) is transformed to the hidden state \(h_0, h_1, ... h_t, ... , h_n\) and the output \(y_0, y_1, ... y_t, ... , y_n\).
The recurrent unit described above is a many-to-many network, since \(n\) input data points are mapped onto \(n\) output data points. By controlling the length of input and output sequences, we may also construct many-to-one, one-to-many networks, and \(m\)-to-\(n\) networks. This is illustrated schematically in Figure 21.3 and can be written algebraically :
Many to one : \[x_0, x_1, ... x_t, ... , x_n \rightarrow y_t\]
One to many :
\[x_t \rightarrow y_0, y_1, ... y_t, ... , y_n\]
Many to many : \[x_0, x_1, ... x_t, ... , x_m \rightarrow y_0, y_1, ... y_t, ... , y_n\]
Early RNNs demonstrated the machines could learn sequential data, including basic language models Mikolov, Karafiát, Burget, Černocký, & Khudanpur (2010).

title: 21  Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
Figure 21.1: A recurrent unit










Figure 21.2: Recurrent unit for several time steps

title: 21  Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
21.2 Backpropagation for Recurrent Networks
The introduction of hidden state makes computation of the gradient of the loss with respect to weights a little more complicated than for standard feedforward networks. However, the procedure becomes clear when we consider the unrolled network shown in Figure 21.2. It should become clear that, much like with backpropagation through a feedforward network, we can write the gradient of the loss using the chain rule, with terms that depend on each time step. The term for the final time step can be computed first, since the gradient does not depend on previous steps. We then proceed to compute gradient terms moving backwards through time steps, hence this is frequently termed “backpropagation through time”.

title: 21  Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
21.3 Shortcomings of RNNs
The vanishing gradient problem was introduced previously. This problem occurs when backpropagation results in the product of many gradient terms \(<<1\). The gradient of the loss can become vanishingly small, resulting in slow training with high computational cost. Since recurrent networks employ backpropagation through time, the vanishing gradient problem may result in constraints on the length of sequences that can be learnt at reasonable computational cost. This was one of the main disadvantages of RNNs, and was alleviated somewhat by the introduction of gated architectures such as the LSTM and GRU, described below.
Another significant disadvantage of recurrent networks is that the forward pass over a sequence cannot be parallelised, since the value of each term in the sequence depends on the previous one. This results in long computation time, with limited possibilities for speeding up, even when significant computational power is available. Again this results in practical limitations on the length of the sequences that can be learnt.

title: 21  Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
21.4 Long Short Term Memory
The Long Short Term Memory (LSTM), introduced in Hochreiter & Schmidhuber (1997), was a highly successful (up to a point) attempt to resolve the vanishing gradient problem which all previous RNNs suffered from. The LSTM relies on the concept of “gating”, which controls the flow of information into and out of a hidden state. It also introduces two hidden states - one (the “cell” state) which captures all the input information in the sequence so far, the other (the “hidden” state), which depends only on the previous time step. The LSTM cell is shown in Figure 21.4. It comprises three gates - the “forget” gate, “input” gate, and “output” gate.






Figure 21.4: The LSTM cell



The LSTM represented a major breakthrough in language modelling in the mid-2010s Sutskever, Vinyals, & Le (2014), and opened up a broad range of time-series problems to machine learning. Applications included forecasting energy demand, financial markets, equipment degradation.

title: 21  Recurrent Neural Networks
text:
21.5 Gated Recurrent Unit
The Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) is a simplified version of the LSTM introduced in Cho et al. (2014). It dispenses with one hidden state, and uses only two gates.






Figure 21.5: The GRU cell



The GRU greatly reduced the computational requirements of LSTMs, allowing applications such as speed recognition on mobile phones, predictive keyboards, battery life prediction.

title: 22  Autoencoders
text:
22.1 Standard Autoencoders
EDIT THIS SECTION
An autoencoder is a neural network trained to reconstruct its own input. It is composed of two parts:
The network is trained, exactly as in Chapter 15, by minimising a loss function — typically Mean Squared Error between the input and its reconstruction:
\[
L = \| \mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}} \|_2^2
\]
using the same L2 norm defined in Section 9.5, and trained by gradient descent (?sec-optimisation) and backpropagation (Section 18.3.2) exactly as for any other network in this unit.
What makes this interesting is that \(\mathbf{z}\) has far fewer dimensions than \(\mathbf{x}\). Since the network is forced to reconstruct the full input from this compressed bottleneck, it must learn a representation that captures the most important structure in the data — the network cannot simply copy the input through unchanged. In this sense, an autoencoder is a form of unsupervised learning (Chapter 17): no labels are required, only the data itself.

title: 22  Autoencoders
text:
An encoder, \(\mathbf{z} = f_{\text{enc}}(\mathbf{x})\), which compresses the input \(\mathbf{x}\) down to a lower-dimensional representation \(\mathbf{z}\), known as the latent code or bottleneck.
A decoder, \(\hat{\mathbf{x}} = f_{\text{dec}}(\mathbf{z})\), which attempts to reconstruct the original input from the latent code alone.






22.1.1 The Connection to PCA
This should sound familiar. If the encoder and decoder are both restricted to be purely linear functions, and the loss is Mean Squared Error, it can be shown that the optimal such autoencoder learns to project the data onto exactly the same subspace as PCA (Chapter 17) — the top \(k\) principal components of the data, found there via eigendecomposition (Chapter 11) or SVD (Section 10.4). A (non-linear) neural network autoencoder is best understood as a direct generalisation of PCA: instead of restricting the compression to a linear projection, the encoder and decoder are allowed to be arbitrarily non-linear functions, letting the network capture curved, non-linear structure in the data that PCA’s flat subspaces cannot.


22.1.2 Limitations for Generation
A standard autoencoder is very good at compression and reconstruction, but it makes a poor generative model — that is, it’s not naturally suited to creating new, realistic examples similar to the training data by sampling from the latent space. The reason is that nothing in the training objective above encourages the latent space to have any particular structure. Points corresponding to real data may be scattered arbitrarily throughout \(\mathbb{R}^k\), with large “gaps” that don’t decode to anything sensible. If you picked a random point \(\mathbf{z}\) and passed it through the decoder, there’s no guarantee you’d get a realistic output at all.
This is precisely the problem the Variational Autoencoder was designed to solve.

title: 22  Autoencoders
text:
22.2 Variational Autoencoders
A Variational Autoencoder (VAE) (Kingma & Welling, 2022) modifies the standard autoencoder in one crucial way: instead of the encoder mapping each input to a single point \(\mathbf{z}\), it maps each input to a probability distribution over the latent space — in practice, almost always a diagonal Gaussian:
\[
q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{z}; \, \boldsymbol{\mu}_\phi(\mathbf{x}), \, \boldsymbol{\sigma}_\phi^2(\mathbf{x}) \right)
\]
The encoder network, with parameters \(\phi\), now outputs two vectors for a given input — a mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and a (log-)variance \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2\) — rather than a single latent code. A sample \(\mathbf{z}\) is then drawn from this distribution and passed to the decoder network, \(p_\theta(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z})\), which attempts the reconstruction just as before.
To make this a genuinely useful generative model, we additionally want the aggregate of all these per-input distributions to fill out the latent space smoothly, with no gaps, so that any point sampled from a simple, known distribution decodes to something realistic. The VAE achieves this by pushing every input’s latent distribution \(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\) towards a fixed, simple prior distribution, almost always chosen to be a standard normal, \(p(\mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, I)\).

22.2.1 The Loss Function: Reconstruction + KL Divergence
This gives the VAE two competing objectives, combined into a single loss function (technically, the negative of a quantity called the Evidence Lower Bound, or ELBO — a direct relative of the log-likelihood objective from ?sec-mle, since a VAE is ultimately trying to maximise the likelihood of the training data under the generative model \(p_\theta\)):
\[
L(\theta, \phi; \mathbf{x}) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_\phi}\big[-\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\big]}_{\text{reconstruction loss}} \; + \; \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x}) \,\|\, p(\mathbf{z})\big)}_{\text{regularisation towards the prior}}
\]

The first term is just the reconstruction error again — for Gaussian-distributed reconstructions this reduces to the same Mean Squared Error used in a standard autoencoder above, and, exactly as shown for supervised regression in ?sec-mle, is itself a negative log-likelihood term in disguise.
The second term, the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, measures how different the encoder’s distribution \(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\) is from the prior \(p(\mathbf{z})\), and penalises the encoder for straying too far from it. This is what forces the latent space, in aggregate across the whole dataset, to fill out smoothly around the origin rather than leaving unstructured gaps.

For two diagonal Gaussians, this KL divergence term has a convenient closed form, so it does not need to be estimated numerically:
\[
D_{\text{KL}}\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2) \,\|\, \mathcal{N}(0,1)\big) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i} \left(1 + \log\sigma_i^2 - \mu_i^2 - \sigma_i^2\right)
\]

import numpy as np

def kl_divergence_to_standard_normal(mu, log_var):
    """KL(N(mu, sigma^2) || N(0, 1)) for a diagonal Gaussian, given log(sigma^2)."""
    return -0.5 * np.sum(1 + log_var - mu**2 - np.exp(log_var))

# a latent distribution that's already close to the prior: small penalty
mu_close = np.array([0.1, -0.05])
logvar_close = np.array([0.0, 0.0])   # sigma^2 = 1
print("KL divergence (close to prior)   :", kl_divergence_to_standard_normal(mu_close, logvar_close))

# a latent distribution far from the prior: larger penalty
mu_far = np.array([3.0, -2.5])
logvar_far = np.array([-1.5, 2.0])    # sigma^2 far from 1
print("KL divergence (far from prior)   :", kl_divergence_to_standard_normal(mu_far, logvar_far))

KL divergence (close to prior)   : 0.006249999999999978
KL divergence (far from prior)   : 10.18109312953954


The tradeoff between these two loss terms is exactly what makes a VAE’s latent space useful: the reconstruction term alone would encourage the encoder to spread inputs far apart in latent space (making reconstruction easier), while the KL term pulls everything back towards a shared, compact, well-structured region — the balance between the two is what produces a latent space where every nearby point decodes to something plausible.


22.2.2 The Reparameterisation Trick
There is a subtlety in training a VAE that is worth making explicit, because it’s a direct, practical application of the chain rule from ?sec-gradients. Sampling \(\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\sigma}^2)\) is a random, non-differentiable operation — gradients cannot flow backwards through a random sampling step during backpropagation (Section 18.3.2), since there is no well-defined derivative of “draw a random sample” with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\).
The fix is to rewrite the sampling step so that all the randomness is isolated in a term that does not depend on the network’s parameters:
\[
\mathbf{z} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_\phi(\mathbf{x}) + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_\phi(\mathbf{x}) \odot \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, I)
\]
where \(\odot\) denotes elementwise multiplication. Now \(\mathbf{z}\) is written as a deterministic, differentiable function of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\), \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\), and a separately-sampled noise term \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) that carries no trainable parameters. This means the chain rule (?sec-gradients) can be applied straight through the sampling step exactly as through any other layer, and the whole network — encoder and decoder together — can be trained end-to-end with ordinary backpropagation.

def reparameterise(mu, log_var, rng):
    sigma = np.exp(0.5 * log_var)
    epsilon = rng.normal(size=mu.shape)
    return mu + sigma * epsilon

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
mu = np.array([1.0, -0.5])
log_var = np.array([0.2, -0.3])

samples = np.array([reparameterise(mu, log_var, rng) for _ in range(5000)])
print("Sample mean     :", samples.mean(axis=0), " (target mu =", mu, ")")
print("Sample variance :", samples.var(axis=0), " (target sigma^2 =", np.exp(log_var), ")")

Sample mean     : [ 1.01267893 -0.49900897]  (target mu = [ 1.  -0.5] )
Sample variance : [1.23696171 0.72564848]  (target sigma^2 = [1.22140276 0.74081822] )


Repeated sampling via this reparameterisation recovers the intended mean and variance, confirming the trick produces samples statistically indistinguishable from directly sampling \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2)\) — while remaining differentiable with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\).


22.2.3 Generating New Data
Once trained, generating a new sample no longer requires an input \(\mathbf{x}\) or the encoder at all: simply draw \(\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, I)\) directly from the prior, and pass it through the decoder, \(\hat{\mathbf{x}} = f_{\text{dec}}(\mathbf{z})\). Because training pushed the aggregate latent distribution to fill out this same prior smoothly, decoded samples from arbitrary points in the prior tend to look like plausible, novel examples from the training distribution, rather than the exact reconstructions of specific training points that a standard autoencoder is limited to.

22.3 Comparison to Other Generative Approaches
VAEs are one of several major families of deep generative model. Two others worth being aware of, though beyond the scope of a detailed treatment here:








Model
Core idea
Notable trait




VAE
Encode to a structured (Gaussian) latent space; decode to reconstruct
Stable to train; latent space is smooth and structured; samples can be somewhat blurry


GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014)
A generator network competes against a discriminator network trying to distinguish real from generated samples
Often sharper samples; training can be unstable (the two networks must remain balanced)


Diffusion models
Learn to reverse a gradual noising process applied to training data
State of the art for image generation as of the early-to-mid 2020s; computationally expensive to sample from



All three ultimately rely on the same underlying toolkit developed across this unit: gradients and the chain rule (?sec-gradients), gradient-based optimisation (?sec-optimisation), and — as made explicit above — maximum likelihood as a guiding principle for what “loss function” even means (?sec-mle).

title: 23  Transformers
text:
23.1 seq2seq
The Transformer architecture has become the dominant architecture for processing sequential data, and is the underlying technology responsible for the boom in generative artificial intelligence during the early 2020s.
Prior to the invention of transformers, processing of sequential data relied on recurrent networks. Despite notable successes, such models suffered from several problems. These included the vanishing gradient and non-parallelisability mentioned previously, but also an inability to handle long range context. A key issue in translation models is identifying the relevant context, for a given output token, within the input sequence. Recurrent models have a tendency to attenuate context from earlier in the sequence, limiting the range over which it can be identified, and hence the length of sentences that can be translated.
Below we describe a successful recurrent model, followed by the key concept of “attention”, before going on to describe the Transformer itself.
The seq2seq model was a highly successful (for the time) recurrent model introduced in 2014 (Sutskever, Vinyals, & Le, 2014). It uses a pair of LSTM networks, in an encoder/decoder architecture, reflecting a view of translation compatible with information theory type models of communication. Use of an end-of-sentence token <eos> allowed the encoder LSTM to convert an arbitrary length sequence into a fixed-size hidden vector. This vector effectively encodes the information contained in the sentence, which is passed to the decoder LSTM for converstion to another arbitrary length sentence (again using the <eos> token).
As for most language models of the time, the input sequence use a one-hot encoding over the input vocabulary. The network output is a softmax, ie. a probability distribution, over the output vocabulary. During training the output ground truth is encoded using a one-hot encoding, allowing a cross-entropy based loss to be calculated.

title: 23  Transformers
text:
23.2 Attention
Attention is a mechanism for determining context in sequence processing. The general concept is that the importance of individual elements (or tokens) in a sequence is encoded in a set of “soft” weights, which are computed during the forward pass. Attention was originally proposed in the context of translation models (Bahdanau, Cho, & Bengio, 2016). For a given decoder hidden state, \(h'_t\), the mechanism aims to determine the importance of each input token, using the encoder hidden state \(h_i\). The original mechanism achieved this using a small neural network, which outputs a score \(e_{t,i}\) for each encoder hidden state. These scores can be converted to a probabilistic basis \(\varepsilon_{t,i}\) using softmax. An example of the attention (ie. the matrix \(\varepsilon_{t,i}\)) is shown in Figure 23.2.






Figure 23.2: Example attention matrix from (Bahdanau et al., 2016)



The attention is used to compute a weighted sum over all the encoder hidden states, known as the context vector : \[c_t = \sum_i \varepsilon_{t,i} h_i\]
The context is computed for each output token and used as additional input to the decoder, as shown diagramatically in Figure 23.3.






Figure 23.3: Attention in a seq2seq architecture




23.2.1 Scaled Dot-product Attention
The original version of attention described above can be computationally quite expensive. Modern approaches to attention use a simplified version which is easier to compute, known as scaled dot-product attention. This approach also introduces an additional concept of storing the input sequence information as a series of \((key,value)\) pairs. This allows each input token (or corresponding hidden state) to be encoded in two ways - one which is optimised for efficient lookup/search, and another which is optimised for use in the context vector. The context vector is then computed using :
\(c_t = {\rm softmax}(\frac{Q_tK^T_i}{\sqrt{d_k}})V_i\)
where the query \(Q_t\) corresponds to the output token for step \(t\), and the input token for step \(i\) is encoded as the key \(K_i\) (for search), and the value \(V_i\) (for context information). The \(Q, K, V\) encodings are supplied by neural networks, allowing the optimal encodings to be learnt during training. The scaling by \(\sqrt(d_k)\), where \(d_k\) is the dimensionality of the input key \(K\), helps correct for reduced effectiveness of scaled dot product attention when \(d_k\) is a large value. The scaled dot production attention mechanism is shown diagramatically in Figure 23.4.






Figure 23.4: Modern scaled dot-product attention, taken from (Vaswani et al., 2023)



The Transformer architecture relies on multi-head attention, shown in Figure 23.5. Here, the attention mechanism is replicated several times, with unique \(Q, K, V\) encodings for each copy. This allows multiple context vectors to be computed, each of which encodes the relationship between elements in input and output sequences, on a unique basis. This reflects the different reasons why words in a sentence can have a relationship with each other.






Figure 23.5: Multi-head attention, taken from (Vaswani et al., 2023)

title: 23  Transformers
text:
23.3 Transformer Architecture
The transformer architecture was introduced in the landmark paper from Google Labs, “Attention is all you need” (Vaswani et al., 2023). Essentially this approach replaced recurrence with ‘just’ attention. The absence of recurrence greatly increases the amount of computation that can be performed concurrently (ie. in parallel). This reduced the training time, and increased the complexity of network (or number of weights) that can be trained. It also means the position of tokens within the input sequence must be encoded at the input, so this information can be used by the network.
The Transformer architecture, shown in Figure 23.6 uses multi-head attention in two ways. The first is ‘self-attention’, which generates a context vector for the input sequence alone. Effectively this encodes the relationship of each element of the sequence to all the other elements. This self-attention mechanism is followed by a deep neural network, and the attention/DNN is repeated several times (6 in the original paper). The output of the stacked attention/DNN block is then sent to a second multi-head attention mechanism, which relates output tokens to input tokens in the same way as described in Section 23.2.
During training, the ground truth output sequence is also sent to a self-attention mechanism in the same way as the input sequence. The input (and ground truth output, during training) is encoded using a one hot encoding. A one hot encoding effectively means each token is represented by a vector of size of the vocabulary, with a 1 in the position of the word to that token. The output of the network is a softmax - effectively a probability distribution over the vocabulary. This allows a cross entropy based loss to be computed and used during training.






Figure 23.6: Transformer architecture, taken from (Vaswani et al., 2023)
